entries.title: Positive limit maneuvering load factor — minimum required value

verification.checked_against: eCFR versioner API, full XML for title-14 § 25.337
verification.notes:
The regulation states a MINIMUM, not an equality: "may not be less than 2.1 + 24,000/(W + 10,000) except that n may not be less than 2.5 and need not be greater than 3.8". Read carefully, that is three separate provisions: a formula, a floor on the required minimum, and a relief cap above which no further increase is required. A design may legitimately use a higher n than this expression yields; treating the result as "the load factor" rather than "the least acceptable load factor" is an engineering choice the regulation does not make. See also 25.337(d), which permits LOWER factors in defined circumstances.
W is specifically the design maximum takeoff weight, not an arbitrary operating weight.

test_cases.description: A design carrying -1.0 exactly meets the requirement. Inputs are the magnitude, which is what the bound is stated on.
A design carrying only -0.5 fails. Under the naive signed reading of the regulation's words (n >= -1.0) this case would have passed, which is the regression this test exists to catch.

entries.title: Negative limit maneuvering load factor up to VC

verification.checked_against: eCFR versioner API, full XML for title-14 § 25.337, issue 2026-07-07, re-read 2026-08-13
verification.notes: Exact text: "The negative limit maneuvering load factor— (1) May not be less than -1.0 at speeds up to VC". Negative is a distinct design condition from the positive case and is frequently omitted when § 25.337 is reduced to its positive formula alone.
verification.sign_convention:
CORRECTED 2026-08-13. This entry previously encoded `operator: "<="` against `value: -1.0` while quoting "may not be less than -1.0" directly above it. Those say opposite things. Read as signed algebra, "not less than -1.0" is n >= -1.0, which would make the WEAKER design (n = -0.5) the compliant one and reject the stronger — plainly not the rule's intent. Read as the airworthiness requirement it is, the airplane must withstand a negative factor of at least 1.0 in magnitude.
The bound is therefore restated on |n_neg|, which is true under either reading and cannot be silently inverted by a consumer's sign convention. The signed equivalent is n_neg <= -1.0 when n_neg is expressed as a negative number; that form is recorded here rather than in the machine field precisely because it depends on a convention the regulation never states.

verification.notes:
"The most severe combination of loads that are likely to arise during a lateral drift landing must be taken into account. In absence of a more rational analysis of this condition, the following must be investigated: (i) A vertical load equal to 75% of the maximum ground reaction of § 25.473 must be considered in combination with a drag and side load of 40% and 25% respectively of that vertical load."
THE ANTECEDENTS ARE DIFFERENT AND IT MATTERS. The vertical is 75% of the MAXIMUM GROUND REACTION; the drag and side are 40% and 25% of THAT REDUCED VERTICAL, not of the maximum. verification.notes:
"The combination of vertical and drag components is considered to be acting at the wheel axle centerline."
A short sentence with a large consequence for support structure. The loads do not arrive at the trunnion as a pure force: applied a strut length below it, drag arrives as a COUPLE of drag times that length, and side load arrives as torsion. Structure that reacts only the force is under-designed by whatever that couple is worth.
EVALUATED ONLY WHEN A STRUT LENGTH IS SUPPLIED, because strut length is a landing gear dimension and this method takes wing geometry. The torsion is not carried at all.

verification.checked_against: eCFR versioner API, full XML for title-14 § 25.535 at issues 2022-01-01 and 2023-06-01, diffed; and the typeset printed CFR (GPO, 14 CFR Ch. I, 1-1-11 edition, p. 418)
verification.notes:
THIS COEFFICIENT WAS WRONG IN THE REGULATION FOR FIFTY-EIGHT YEARS.
From the 1964 original until 2022 the section read "a side component equal to 3.25 tan beta". Amdt. 25-148 (87 FR 75710, 9 December 2022, corrected at 88 FR 2813, 18 January 2023) changed it to 0.25 tan beta as part of a Miscellaneous Amendments rule addressing typographical and editorial errors. The 2011 printed CFR still shows 3.25.
The correction is a THIRTEENFOLD REDUCTION in the unsymmetrical step side load. Any tool, textbook or type-certification basis built on a pre-2023 copy of Part 25 carries the larger figure. That the error stood for fifty-eight years, in a paragraph whose sibling (e) had 0.25 all along, is the strongest argument in this corpus for the `edition` field being mandatory on every entry.
Concretely, on the wing-tip float of cfr-25.535-b-step-load's worked case — L = 19329.35 lb at 20 degrees deadrise — the side load is 1758.83 lb under the rule in force and 22864.75 lb under the text that stood until 2022.
The 0.25 value is also what harmonises (d) with (e), with cfr-25.529-b1-unsymmetrical-side-component for hulls, and with § 25.529(c) for twin floats, all of which use 0.25 tan beta.
A SEPARATE DEFECT REMAINS, UNCORRECTED. The paragraph takes 0.75 times "the load specified in paragraph (a)", but (a) is the General paragraph and specifies no load at all; the step load is in (b). The 2022 pass fixed the coefficient in this sentence and left the dangling reference beside it. Read as written the vertical component is undefined. This corpus binds it to the (b) step load, which is what (e) does for the bow case and the only reading that makes the paragraph operable — an engineering reading, not a regulatory one.

This is the only water load formula in Subpart C written in genuine physical quantities — it contains an explicit rho and a dynamic-pressure form (rho/2) * area * speed^2 — rather than being an empirical fit whose constants silently absorb the units. entries.title: INTERPRETATION: speed units in the immersed float drag and side components

verification.checked_against: Not resolvable from 14 CFR. The stated unit was confirmed to be "knots" in two independent renderings of the section — the current eCFR XML and the typeset printed CFR (GPO, 14 CFR Ch. I, 1-1-11 edition, p. 418) — so it is not an eCFR artifact. No FAA advisory material, and no primary source consulted, states which unit closes the equation.
verification.notes:
WHAT IS ESTABLISHED, from the printed CFR rather than inferred:
rho is slugs/ft^3 and V is ft^3. The eCFR XML renders both as "ft.2", which the typeset CFR shows to be a mangled superscript. An earlier revision of this corpus reached the same conclusion by dimensional analysis alone; it is now read from the source, per the Round 2 process change.
WHY THE UNIT MATTERS AND WHY IT CANNOT BE READ OFF THE PAGE:
This is the only water load expression in Subpart C written in genuine physical quantities. Every other one — cfr-25.527-a1, cfr-25.533-b1-keel-pressure, cfr-25.535-b-step-load — is an empirical fit whose constant silently absorbs the units, which is why knots is unremarkable there. Here the form is C * (rho/2) * area * speed^2, the textbook dynamic pressure, and C_x and C_y are called "coefficient of drag force" and "coefficient of side force" — the language of dimensionless coefficients, not of fitted constants. Such an expression closes on slug/ft^3 * ft^2 * (ft/s)^2 = lbf and on nothing else.
The companion component in the same load set settles that the drafters were working in consistent units: cfr-25.535-f-immersed-vertical is rho * g * V, which is exactly lbf with rho in slug/ft^3 and V in ft^3 and needs no fitted constant at all. One load set cannot coherently use consistent units for its vertical component and knots for its horizontal ones.
Against that, the section plainly says knots, and it survived a targeted FAA technical-corrections pass over this very section in 2022 — Amdt. 25-148 fixed a genuine typo in paragraph (d) and left paragraph (f) alone. That is real evidence, though a corrections pass fixes what has been reported rather than everything that is wrong.
THE CHOICE MADE HERE, AND WHY:
ft/s. Two reasons, in order. First, it is the only reading under which the expression is the drag equation it visibly is. Second, it is the conservative one for a strength requirement: it yields loads 1.68781^2 = 2.849 times larger, and a float strut sized to the larger number satisfies the smaller. Choosing the other way round would be choosing the unconservative reading of an ambiguous rule.
This is an INTERPRETATION and is labelled one. A certification programme must obtain FAA agreement rather than rely on this entry; § 25.521(b) makes the whole method defeasible by a more rational analysis in any case. If the FAA ever states the unit, this entry gets retracted in docs/verification-log.md rather than quietly edited.

variables.description: Displaced volume the float must provide
Maximum weight of the seaplane or amphibian. Note "maximum weight", not "maximum design landing weight" — see cfr-25.751-a-main-float-buoyancy.
Fresh water density. ENGINEERING VALUE, not regulatory. 62.4 lb/ft^3 is the conventional figure.

test_cases.description: Displaced volume for a single main float, fresh water
The same airframe as a twin float installation, each float sized for half the weight per 25.525(c). Half the volume each, so no margin is gained or lost by the split.

entries.title: INTERPRETATION: displaced volume implied by the 25.751(a) buoyancy margin

verification.checked_against: The 1.8 multiplier is regulatory (25.751(a), verified). The conversion from a buoyancy requirement to a displaced volume is not: it needs a water density, and § 25.751 specifies none.
verification.notes:
Split out of cfr-25.751-a-main-float-buoyancy, where it had been carried as a worked example inside an otherwise purely regulatory entry. That placement let a non-regulatory constant (62.4 lb/ft3) inherit the parent entry's `verified` status by adjacency.
Two engineering choices are folded in here and neither is in the rule. Fresh water density is taken as 62.4 lb/ft3 at about 60 F; it varies with temperature, and salt water is roughly 64 lb/ft3, which makes this the conservative choice for the fresh-water condition the section names. And the form below assumes the float alone supports the full maximum weight — for twin-float configurations see cfr-25.525-c-twin-float-equivalent-hull, under which each float is sized for half the seaplane weight.

entries.statement: Positive transverse metacentric height (GM > 0) in the two-compartment-flooded condition is commonly used as a computable proxy for 25.755(a). It is an interpretation, not a regulatory requirement.
entries.title: INTERPRETATION: positive transverse metacentric height as a proxy criterion

verification.checked_against: Not present in 14 CFR 25.755. Included explicitly so that downstream users do not mistake it for regulatory text.
verification.notes: GM > 0 is a conventional naval-architecture proxy for "positive stability" and is a reasonable engineering criterion, but the regulation states a qualitative probability-minimization standard, not a metacentric height threshold. Any tool asserting GM > 0 as the Part 25 compliance criterion is substituting an interpretation for the rule. Flagged, not endorsed.
